Actually, this isn't true. Sim games are some of the most comfortable VR experiences out there. Being inside something helps a lot as you have a stationary reference that helps prevent VR sickness from happening in the majority of users.

This is why a newer feature in several VR games is a 'cage' option that puts your avatar inside a cage that provides that same reference and helps curb the problem with VR movement. Games that feature helmets with visible glass or static HUD displays also help with this issue.

There is no cure all for everyone, but most people can handle VR just fine, particularly if they are inside a vehicle or have some other form of static reference to help the eyes and brain cope with it.

Also, VR sickness and motion sickness aren't the same thing. They actually have exact opposite causes, even though symptoms are similar they are different things.

People who get motion sick easily won't necessarily experience VR sickness. I'd still go in cautiously if you do, but it's not a given that someone sensitive to one will be sensitive to the other.

Motion sickness is caused by contradictory inputs in your sensory system. Your inner ear contains fluid in a series of tubes. When you move, the fluid moves and bends hairs inside the tubes in the inner ear. This in turn sends signals to the brain which interpret this movement. This is the telemetry that allows us to maintain balance.

Of course, your ears are only part of the picture. You also gather movement data via sight. When what you see doesn't line up with the other sensory data this can cause confusion in the brain which may manifest as motion sickness. What you describe as "VR sickness" isn't the opposite of motion sickness, it IS motion sickness. With motion sickness it's that you're moving but some part of your sensory apparatus is saying "no you aren't". With "VR sickness" your inner ear is saying you aren't moving, but another part of your sensory apparatus is saying "yes you are". The fact that this is reversed doesn't really make it a different thing because it's the discrepancy that is causing it and the effects are exactly the same.

Some people have the ability to ignore larger amounts of the false input, while others do not. This is why some people seem susceptible to it while others are seemingly unaffected. In reality, everyone is prone to motion sickness. It's just a question of how much of a discrepancy you can withstand before physical symptoms manifest.

Yeah. No. I gave an extremely simplified explanation, but they are not the same thing.

If they are the same, then why is VR sickness considered a different thing in the case of medical study of it?

There are a lot of theories about why it happens, and while we have a pretty good grasp on what causes it, we're not sure that we have the full picture yet. It is no doubt closely related to Motion Sickness, but it has been established as a different thing.

Part of the reason behind VR sickness has nothing to do with the issues that cause motion sickness. Low or inconsistent framerate and high persistence are also related to it. The flicker of the screen and delay between when the user moves their head and when it displays on the screen are also factors.

A VR user can get VR sickness even if they are wearing the VR device and are literally moving around in a 1 to 1 ratio within a simulated environment. In other words, completely eliminating the visual/movement disconnect that causes motion sickness.

If it was simply motion sickness, then providing a static reference wouldn't help, but it's been proven that it does in many cases.

VR sickness symptoms also tend to linger longer, and no one is sure why exactly.

So no, they are not the same thing, and while some of the causes are similar and they are likely related on some level, there are other factors involved with VR sickness that have no relation to motion sickness at all. The fact that opposite sensations help trigger it is only part of why they aren't the same thing.

Hell yes. This sort of game is the best reason to own one in my opinion. I frequently use mine to play these sorts of games.

Elite Dangerous, Sublevel Zero, Eve Valkyrie, Descent Underground all work with VR. Star Citizen is saying it will also be compatible with it, though I'm unsure of the current state of that.

DCS World, War Thunder, and Aeroflight FS 2 are all VR compatible for more traditional flight sims. Plus, Lunar Flight is an oddball addition that also features native VR support.

Project Cars, Dirt Rally, iRacing, Live for Speed, and Assetto Corsa are amazing in VR, especially with a wheel. Plus Euro Truck Simulator 2 is also a lot of fun.

I also highly recommend No Limits 2, which is a roller coaster simulator that not only allows you to build your own theme park with various rides and design your own roller coasters that you can hop on in VR, but also lets you download and ride the creations of others. This is an essential sim for a VR owner, as it's an endless supply of roller coasters, many of which would be impossible to create in real life.

Minecraft Windows 10 edition works in VR natively and there's a mod that adds it to regular Minecraft, visiting some of the build servers in VR is amazing. I particularly recommend the Middle Earth and Disney World servers, but there's lots of other cool stuff to check out.

If you're into sim style games, VR is totally worth it.
